executiveSummary: Chapter 20 addresses the accounting and financial reporting of defined benefit pension plans and other postretirement benefits under IAS 19, focusing on how employers measure and recognise the pension obligation (defined benefit obligation), pension expense (service cost and net interest), and remeasurements. The chapter concludes that full and immediate recognition of all changes in the net defined benefit obligation—with remeasurements routed through other comprehensive income rather than net income—provides the most transparent and decision-useful information for financial statement users.
keyTopics: Defined Contribution vs. Defined Benefit Plans: A defined contribution plan fixes only the employer's periodic contribution; the employee bears investment risk. A defined benefit plan specifies the retirement benefit formula, leaving the employer responsible for any funding shortfall and making accounting significantly more complex.

Measures of the Pension Obligation: Three alternative measures exist—vested benefit obligation (vested benefits at current salaries), accumulated benefit obligation (all service at current salaries), and defined benefit obligation (all service at projected future salaries); IAS 19 mandates use of the defined benefit obligation as the most representationally faithful measure.

Net Defined Benefit Obligation (Asset) and Funded Status: The funded status equals the defined benefit obligation minus the fair value of plan assets; a positive result is a pension liability and a negative result is a pension asset, both reported on the statement of financial position under the net approach.

Components of Pension Expense: Pension expense has two income-statement components—current service cost (increase in the DBO from employee service this period) and net interest (discount rate multiplied by the net funded status at the start of the period); both affect net income.

Past Service Cost: When a plan is amended to grant additional retroactive benefits, or curtailed, the resulting change in the DBO (past service cost) is recognised immediately as pension expense in the period of the amendment or curtailment, with no deferral or amortisation.

Remeasurements (Asset and Liability Gains/Losses): The difference between actual return on plan assets and assumed interest revenue is an asset gain or loss; changes in the DBO from revised actuarial assumptions are liability gains or losses. Both are recognised immediately in other comprehensive income (OCI) and are never recycled to net income under IFRS.

Pension Worksheet: A working tool (not part of the general ledger) that tracks formal journal entry columns alongside memo columns for the DBO and plan assets, ensuring the ending Pension Asset/Liability balance always reconciles to the net funded status.

IFRS vs. U.S. GAAP Differences: Under U.S. GAAP, past service cost is amortised over remaining service lives, and remeasurements accumulate in AOCI and are amortised using the corridor approach; under IFRS, both are recognised immediately (PSC in net income; remeasurements in OCI with no recycling).

importantDefinitions.Defined Benefit Obligation (DBO): The present value of expected future benefit payments earned by employees for service in current and prior periods, calculated using projected future salary levels; the measure of pension liability required by IAS 19.
importantDefinitions.Defined Benefit Plan: A pension arrangement that specifies the retirement benefit formula (typically a function of years of service and final salary), placing investment and longevity risk on the employer.
importantDefinitions.Defined Contribution Plan: A pension arrangement in which the employer agrees only to contribute a specified amount each period; the ultimate benefit depends on amounts contributed and investment performance, with risk borne by the employee.
importantDefinitions.Net Defined Benefit Obligation (Asset): The funded status of the plan, calculated as DBO minus the fair value of plan assets; reported as a pension liability (if positive) or pension asset (if negative) on the statement of financial position.
importantDefinitions.Service Cost: The increase in the present value of the DBO resulting from employee service; current service cost relates to the current period, while past service cost relates to prior periods arising from a plan amendment or curtailment.
importantDefinitions.Net Interest: The financing component of pension expense, calculated by multiplying the discount rate by the net defined benefit obligation (asset) at the beginning of the period; reported in the financing section of the income statement.
importantDefinitions.Remeasurements: Gains and losses arising from (1) the difference between actual return on plan assets and assumed interest revenue, and (2) changes in actuarial assumptions affecting the DBO; recognised in OCI and not recycled to net income.
importantDefinitions.Past Service Cost (PSC): The change in the DBO caused by a plan amendment (introducing or changing benefits) or curtailment (significant reduction in employees covered); recognised immediately as pension expense.
importantDefinitions.Projected Unit Credit Method: The actuarial valuation method required by IAS 19 that allocates projected pension benefits to periods of service and incorporates expected future salary levels in measuring the DBO; also called the benefits/years-of-service method.
importantDefinitions.Asset Ceiling: The upper limit on the pension asset that may be recognised on the statement of financial position, equal to the present value of economic benefits available to the employer through refunds or reductions in future contributions.
importantDefinitions.Curtailment: A significant reduction in the number of employees covered by a pension plan, treated the same as a plan amendment for accounting purposes and giving rise to past service cost.
importantDefinitions.Vested Benefits: Benefits that an employee is entitled to receive even if he or she renders no additional service to the employer; the basis for the most conservative measure of the pension obligation.

accountingTreatments: Recognition of pension liability/asset: At each reporting date, the net defined benefit obligation (DBO less fair value of plan assets) is recognised as a pension liability or pension asset on the statement of financial position. If the plan is overfunded, the recognised asset is the lower of the surplus and the asset ceiling.

Pension expense journal entry (annual): Dr. Pension Expense [service cost + net interest] / Dr. or Cr. Pension Asset/Liability [difference between expense and cash contributed] / Cr. Cash [employer contribution]. Example (Zarle AG 2022): Dr. Pension Expense €9,000 | Cr. Cash €8,000 | Cr. Pension Asset/Liability €1,000.

Past service cost: Recognised entirely in the period of plan amendment or curtailment. Dr. Pension Expense [PSC amount] / Cr. Defined Benefit Obligation [same amount]. For Zarle AG 2023: Dr. Pension Expense €81,600 | Cr. DBO €81,600.

Remeasurement—asset gain/loss: If actual return > assumed interest revenue, debit Plan Assets and credit OCI (G/L) for the gain; if actual return < assumed interest revenue, debit OCI (G/L) and credit Plan Assets for the loss. These entries never pass through net income.

Remeasurement—liability gain/loss: If actuarial assumptions increase the DBO beyond the computed balance, debit OCI (G/L) and credit DBO for the liability loss; a decrease gives a liability gain in the opposite direction. For Zarle AG 2024 liability loss: Dr. OCI (G/L) €26,594 | Cr. DBO €26,594.

Presentation in comprehensive income: Service cost and net interest are included in net income (operating and financing sections respectively). Remeasurements (asset and liability gains/losses) are included in other comprehensive income, accumulating in Accumulated OCI in equity; they are never reclassified (recycled) to net income in subsequent periods.
criticalFormulas: Net Defined Benefit Obligation (Funded Status) = Defined Benefit Obligation − Fair Value of Plan Assets. Example: DBO €4,000,000 − Plan Assets €3,700,000 = Pension Liability €300,000.

Net Interest = (DBO × Discount Rate) − (Plan Assets × Discount Rate) = Net Funded Status × Discount Rate. Example (Zarle 2022, equal DBO and assets of €100,000 at 10%): Interest expense €10,000 − Interest revenue €10,000 = Net interest €0.

Pension Expense (income statement) = Current Service Cost + Past Service Cost (if any) + Net Interest. Example (Zarle 2023): €9,500 + €81,600 + (€193,600 × 10% − €111,000 × 10%) = €9,500 + €81,600 + €8,260 = €99,360.

Actual Return on Plan Assets = (Ending Plan Assets − Beginning Plan Assets) − (Contributions − Benefits Paid). Example (Hasbro SA): (€4,460,000 − €4,200,000) − (€300,000 − €250,000) = €260,000 − €50,000 = €210,000.

Asset Gain (Loss) = Actual Return on Plan Assets − Assumed Interest Revenue (Plan Assets × Discount Rate). Example (Shopbob SE, 2022): Actual return €8,000 − (€100,000 × 6%) = €8,000 − €6,000 = Asset Gain €2,000.
Liability Loss (Gain) = Actuarially Determined DBO − Computed DBO (before remeasurement). Example (Zarle 2024): Actuary-determined DBO €265,000 − Computed DBO €238,406 = Liability Loss €26,594.
illustrativeExample: Zarle AG 3-year pension illustration (2022–2024): Beginning 2022, DBO and plan assets are both €100,000 (funded status = €0). Service cost €9,000, net interest €0 (equal assets and liabilities), contributions €8,000 → Pension Expense €9,000, cash €8,000, Pension Liability €1,000. In 2023, plan amended granting PSC €81,600; service cost €9,500; net interest €8,260; contributions €20,000 → Pension Expense €99,360, Pension Liability grows to €80,360. In 2024, service cost €13,000; net interest €8,036; actual return €12,000 vs. assumed €13,410 (asset loss €1,410); actuarial DBO adjustment €26,594 (liability loss) → Pension Expense €21,036 in net income, OCI charge €28,004 (remeasurements), Pension Liability €105,400 and Accumulated OCI €28,004 reported on the statement of financial position.
disclosurePresentationNotes: Reconciliation schedules required: Companies must disclose a full roll-forward reconciliation of the DBO and plan assets from beginning to ending balance, showing service cost, interest, PSC, contributions, benefits paid, and remeasurements separately; the funded status (pension asset/liability) must also be reconciled.

Sensitivity analysis: For each significant actuarial assumption (e.g., discount rate, salary growth rate, mortality), companies must disclose the effect on the DBO of a reasonably possible change in that assumption at the reporting date, along with the methods and limitations of those analyses.

Future cash flow information: Required disclosures include (a) the funding policy and arrangements, (b) expected contributions for the next reporting period, and (c) a maturity profile or distribution of the timing of benefit payments.

Remeasurements in OCI—no recycling: IFRS prohibits reclassifying (recycling) pension-related OCI items into net income in future periods; the cumulative balance in Accumulated OCI is reported in the equity section of the statement of financial position and may be transferred to other equity accounts but never back through the income statement.
potentialPitfalls: Confusing DBO with accumulated benefit obligation: IAS 19 requires the defined benefit obligation (using projected future salaries), not the accumulated benefit obligation (using current salaries). Using current salaries understates both the pension liability and annual service cost, particularly for younger workforces with significant expected wage growth.

Treating remeasurements as pension expense: Asset gains/losses (actual vs. assumed return) and liability gains/losses (actuarial assumption changes) must go to OCI, not net income. Routing them through pension expense overstates or understates reported earnings and violates IAS 19's explicit prohibition on recycling; this is a common error when transitioning from U.S. GAAP, which uses the corridor amortisation approach.

Applying the asset ceiling incorrectly when the plan is overfunded: When plan assets exceed the DBO, the pension asset recognised on the statement of financial position is capped at the lower of the surplus and the asset ceiling (present value of refunds or future contribution reductions available to the employer). Recognising the full surplus without testing the ceiling overstates assets and equity.

sources: Learning Objective 1 — Fundamentals of Pension Plan Accounting: covers pension plan types, actuarial role, DBO measurement alternatives, funded status, and the three components of changes in net defined benefit obligation (IAS 19).

Learning Objectives 2–4 — Pension Worksheet, Past Service Cost, and Remeasurements: illustrated via the multi-year Zarle AG case (2022–2025) demonstrating formal journal entries, PSC immediate recognition, and OCI treatment of asset/liability gains and losses.

Learning Objectives 5–6 — Financial Statement Reporting and Other Postretirement Benefits: covers statement of financial position classification, AOCI presentation, reconciliation note disclosures (Illustration 20.25–20.26), and the application of identical accounting principles to healthcare and other non-pension postretirement benefits.
